title: Bridging the AI Literacy Gap
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky argues that schools have drifted into classroom uses of generative AI without teaching general AI literacy to students or staff. Early deterrence-style policies are proving unenforceable, students are teaching themselves in private, and teachers lack training and curriculum. His proposed remedy is a short AI literacy sequence built on a cultural studies approach. Step one asks students about their own and their families' histories, hopes and fears about AI and listens before teaching. Step two has them sort public hot takes into techno-idealist, techno-realist and techno-pessimist orientations. Only after establishing self and society does the course move to how AI works and how to use it. The piece is a school-level program proposal rather than an evidence report, but it is squarely about AI in classrooms and offers a concrete starting sequence.
points: Teachers use occasional classroom AI activities as a stand-in for AI literacy instruction, leaving a gap in both student and staff understanding.
First-round deterrence policies are ineffective, and students' private AI use is creating implicit norms that undermine school rules.
The first step is to ask students about their histories with computing and AI and to listen, not to lecture or turn them loose on a tool.
Students' twin fears of job loss and deference to machine authority can be addressed by a narrative that places human feedback at the center.
A three-way orientation of techno-idealism, realism and pessimism gives students a way to categorise and critique AI hot takes.
quotes: Instead, most educators, pressed for time and by other curricular demands, use these impromptu Gen AI appearances in their courses of study as stand-ins for general AI literacy instruction.

Students are conflicted about these uses, but feel a need to master these tools in the absence of direct instruction. This use is creating implicit norms that will continue to subvert existing school policies in complicated and unpredictable ways, and until there is more transparency on both sides of the equation, nothing like a lasting and satisfying solution will be achievable.

First, students worry about their own job prospects in a world bent toward greater automation. All the talk of job elimination is trickling down not so slowly into the classroom. Students are validly wondering why they are working so hard to learn math, writing, etc. when computers appear to do similar tasks so efficiently and accurately.
No person responds to Gen AI in a vacuum. Every response emerges in a context and is a continuation of a history. All these statements are very much the case for our students.

The implicit goal of this overview is to both relativize and contextualize the heated opinions about AI that circulate around school, on social media, in film and television, at home, etc. By the end of this second stage of AI literacy work, students should feel better equipped to categorize different “hot takes” on Gen AI as representative of different approaches or schools.

Techno-Realism: Evaluates Gen AI developments on their merits and in context. Cautious about AGI labeling, focuses on short-term gains and risks, and recognizes humans' historical ability to navigate technology's impact.

Really, a school just needs 2-3 interested teachers or administrators who can dedicate some time to developing a program, and the courage to commit to training staff and faculty on that program in some kind of holistic manner.
